Droit de la famille — 25474

2025 QCCS 1295

SUPERIOR COURT

CANADA

PROVINCE OF QUEBEC

DISTRICT OF

TERREBONNE

No:

700-12-054215-231

DATE:

April 7, 2025

_____________________________________________________________________

BY

THE HONOURABLE

FLORENCE LUCAS, J.S.C.

_____________________________________________________________________

H. R.

Plaintiff

v.

N. A.

Defendant

_____________________________________________________________________

JUDGMENT

_____________________________________________________________________

[
1
]

H. R. (
Plaintiff
) and N. A. (
Defendant
)
are both of the Iranian Shia Muslim faith. They got married on June 19, 2014,
in Iran. They landed together in Canada in August 2019.

[
2
]

The Plaintiff served the Defendant with an
Application
for divorce
on August 4, 2023, which was modified on October 2, 2023 to add
submissions based on
section 21.1
of the
Divorce Act
[1]
, specified
in the
Demand to lift the religious barriers to remarry, to lift the travel
ban and damages
filed on January 13, 2025 (
Plaintiff’s Demand
)
[2]
.

[
3
]

She claims that the Defendant withholds, without
valid ground, his consent to grant the religious and Iranian divorce. This has
the effect of restricting the Plaintiff from travelling to her country of
origin to see her family, as she

could not leave Iran
without the Defendant’s permission, according to the
Iranian Passport
Law
[3]
.

[
4
]

More specifically, the Plaintiff asks this
Court to :

GRANT
the present application;

ORDER
the Defendant to grant the Plaintiff her religious and Iranian
Divorce and register it before the Iranian authorities;

ORDER
the Defendant to lift the travel ban against the Plaintiff;

ORDER
all the Defendant’s demands, pleadings, defence and counter demands
before the Superior Court in the present divorce file be dismissed unless he
provides the Plaintiff with the mandate she needs to apply for and obtain an
Iranian divorce herself for the benefit of them both;

ORDER
the Defendant to pay for damages in the amount of $100 per day since
August 4th, 2023, in case the Defendant delays or refuses to grant and register
the Plaintiff’s religious and Iranian Divorce from the day of issuing of this
judgment;

CONDEMN
the Defendant to punitive damages of $ 2 000;

ORDER
that the sum to be paid by the Defendant to the Plaintiff be paid
with legal interest at and the additional indemnity pursuant to the provisions
of article 1619 C.C.Q. from the service of the application;

THE WHOLE
with costs against the Defendant.

[
5
]

In his defence, the Defendant argues that he does
not impose any restriction to the Plaintiff and it is not feasible nor within
his control to proceed with the Plaintiff’s demand, since the religious divorce
depends on judicial and religious institutions, according to
section 21.1(6)
of
the
Divorce Act
.

[
6
]

Each party provides an expert opinion and report
on Iranian family law and Sharia law, to advise the Court on the procedures
that must be followed to obtain an Iranian religious divorce
[4]
.

ANALYSIS

[
7
]

Section 21.1
of the
Divorce Act
gives the
Court discretionary power in cases where a spouse refuses to grant a religious
divorce, in order to use it as a bargaining tool in civil divorce proceedings
[5]
.

[
8
]

The Court has no jurisdiction to grant a
religious divorce. However, when the barriers are not removed after the period
allowed by the Court, it may, in any terms that the Court considers
appropriate, dismiss any application filed by that spouse under the
Divorce
Act
, and strike out any other his/her pleadings and affidavits (
sec.
21.1(3)
). In addition, a former spouse’s refusal engages his/her personal
extracontractual civil liability and therefore, may constitute a fault giving
rise to damages, including punitive damages for unlawful and intentional
interference with the other spouse right and freedom
[6]
.

[
9
]

This provision does not apply where the refusal
is based on serious grounds of a religious or conscientious nature (sec. 21.1(4)).

[
10
]

This Court's discretionary power can only be
used when the decision is entirely in the hands of one or both spouses and not
when the power to remove the barrier to religious remarriage lies with a
religious body or official (
sec. 21.1
.(6)).

[
11
]

More particularly, in
Bruker v. Marcovitz
[7]
, Justice
Abella, speaking for the majority of the Supreme court, explains the objective
of this section :

[5]      For an observant Jewish woman
in Canada, this presents a dichotomous scenario: under Canadian law, she is
free to divorce her husband regardless of his consent; under Jewish law,
however, she remains married to him unless he gives his

consent.
This means that while she can remarry under Canadian law, she is prevented from
remarrying in accordance with her religion.  The inability to do so, for
many Jewish women, results in the loss of their ability to remarry at all.

[6]      The vast majority
of Jewish husbands freely give their wives a
get
. Those who do not,
however, represent a long-standing source of concern and frustration in Jewish
communities […].

[7]      In response to these
concerns, after consultation with the leaders of 50 religious groups in Canada
and with the specific agreement of the Roman Catholic, Presbyterian and
Anglican churches, in 1990 the then Minister of Justice, Doug Lewis, introduced
amendments to the
Divorce Act

, R.S.C. 1985, c. 3 (2nd Supp

.), Bill C-61, giving a court discretionary authority to prevent a
spouse from obtaining relief under the Act if that spouse refused to remove a
barrier to religious remarriage (
s. 21.1
).  At second reading, the
Minister outlined the motivation for these amendments, explaining:

The bill before us today is an amendment to the
Divorce Act

which would provide a court with
discretionary powers to preclude a spouse from obtaining relief or proceeding
under the
Divorce Act

where that spouse refuses to
remove a barrier to religious remarriage and where the power to remove the
barrier to religious remarriage lies solely with that person.  Where the
court is satisfied that the spouse who refuses to remove the barrier has
genuine grounds of a religious or conscientious nature for doing so, it need
not exercise its discretion to grant the remedy provided for in this
legislation.

. . .
A spouse should not be able
to refuse to participate in a Jewish religious divorce — called a Get — in
order to obtain concessions in a civil divorce.  The Get should not be
used as a bargaining tool for child custody and access or monetary support
.
[…]

. . .

It is the case that
in some
religions, the Roman Catholic, Greek Orthodox and Islam, annulment or divorce
may proceed more easily and faster if the couple agree
.

However, in all these cases, the
authority to grant the annulment or divorce rests with the religious tribunal,
not the couple.

An uncooperative spouse may delay a
decision, but ultimately, he or she cannot prevent the religious tribunal from
rendering its decision.

In these religions, the spouse
initiating the action can ask the religious authorities to deal with this
problem.

The Jewish spouse does not have
that recourse. […]

[references
omitted]

[
12
]

Notwithstanding the aforementioned opinion of
the Minister of Justice
[8]
,
the
Divorce Act
does not specify that the
section 21.1
of the
Divorce
Act
applies only for the purpose of obtaining a
Get
in the Jewish
faith. Moreover, Quebec courts have used this discretionary power for other
religious confessions, including religious divorce in accordance with the
Iranian and Shia Muslim faith
[9]
.

[
13
]

In the present case, no application for divorce
has been made in Iran. Nevertheless, it is important to understand that under
the provisions of the
Civil Code of Iran
, the right to divorce is
granted to men, whenever they wish to do so
[10]
.
It prevents women from initiating divorce proceedings, except in limited
situations (among others, his marriage to another woman, husband’s absence for
a certain period, attempted murder of the wife, harsh treatment making life
together unbearable, hatred of the wife towards her husband or mutual dislike, and
also, renunciation by the wife of her Mahr
[11]

subject to the husband's consent to divorce
[12]
).

[
14
]

Unfortunately, the circumstances of the present
case do not fall within any of the situations allowing the Plaintiff to apply herself
for a divorce before the Iranian court.

[
15
]

In contrast, under Canadian law, a woman is free
to divorce her husband regardless of his consent
[13]
.

[
16
]

In Iran, divorce takes place once the following
mandatory steps are completed. The first step, the application before the civil
court (
civil divorce
), is a decision from the competent court called as
the issuance of a
Certificate of Impossibility to Reconciliation
[14]
, which
serves as an authorization from court to proceed with the second step, the
religious divorce.

[
17
]

In other words, the Defendant’s expert explains
that “the legally recognized form of divorce is religious divorce, while the
civil procedure serves as a preliminary legal and obligatory step to obtain
judicial authorization”. Consequently, in Iran, “religious divorce cannot be
granted without a prior court decision, as the pronouncement of divorce (recitation
of the relevant Quranic verse) is contingent upon the court's ruling”
[15]
. Once pronounced, the
religious divorce must be registered in the
Marriage and Divorce Registry
Office
[16]
.

[
18
]

Outside Iran, according to section 15 of the
Iranian
Family Protection Law
[17]
,
“divorce judgments issued by foreign courts at the
request of an Iranian citizen residing abroad are not automatically recognized
or enforceable in Iran. Such judgments will only be executed if they fully
comply with the requirements stipulated in Iranian law, including the
Civil
Code
,
Penal Code
, and the
Family Protection Law
. A competent
Iranian court must review and assess the divorce in light of Iranian legal
principles and Islamic law”
[18]
.

[
19
]

In the present case, as it is the Plaintiff who
filed the divorce application before the Quebec Superior Court, it is likely
that the Iranian court will refuse to grant recognition and ratify the divorce
judgment to be rendered, because it would be contrary to Iranian law as it would
infringe the Defendant's right to initiate divorce unilaterally and exclusively
[19]
.

[
20
]

Then, Plaintiff has no significant chance of
obtaining a civil and religious divorce in Iran
[20]
. And
even if she has a Canadian civil divorce judgment, she will be considered
married to the Defendant in Iran, and consequently, she will not be able to
leave Iran without the Defendant’s permission
[21]
.
Moreover, should the Plaintiff start a relationship with another man, she can not
remarry and can be accused of adultery with a potential sentence of capital
punishment by stoning
[22]
.

[
21
]

However, a “Note” to section 15 of the
Family
Protection Law
sets out an other option for the Iranians outside Iran: “It
is possible to register divorces of Iranians residing aboard in the consulates
of the Islamic Republic of Iran upon written
request of the spouses or the
husband
by presenting a certificate of execution of the divorce decree by
the
authorized persons
who are introduced to the consulates upon the
proposal of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs and the approval of the Head of the
Judiciary”
[23]
.

[
22
]

The Plaintiff’s expert produces a list of “Names
of individuals [Imams] licensed by the Judiciary of the Islamic Republic of
Iran for the purpose of performing the Islamic divorce ceremony, based on the
Note to section 15 of the
Family Protection Law
”
[24]
.

[
23
]

According to this Note, two conditions are
required : 1) a written request from the spouses or the husband, and 2) the presentation
of a certificate of execution of the divorce granted by an licensed Imam. There
are two key points to make. First, if the wife is the party requesting the
religious divorce, the Imam cannot grant the certificate unless the husband
consents. Second, the divorce judgment is not specifically requested.

[
24
]

The Defendant refuses to sign the documents
regarding the religious divorce before obtaining the civil divorce in Canada.
He alleges that “a Town A Imam has advised that, in accordance with the principles
of the Shia Muslim faith, he will not take any action regarding a religious
divorce unless all issues relating to the parties’ marriage have been fully
resolved
[25]
.”
No affidavit in support of theses allegations has been produced and the Imam
was not called upon to testify. Consequently, the Imam's declaration consists
of hearsay and is inadmissible in evidence to prove the truth of its content.

[
25
]

The Plaintiff’s expert explains that for the
Iranians residing outside of Iran, if the spouses agree on the divorce, they present themselves at a registered Imam’s office, and the husband
gives the Imam power to perform the Islamic divorce ceremony on his behalf. According
to her experience, the licensed Imam can perform the ceremony before the civil
divorce. As an example, she provides
the documents from the
Islamic Education Center
in Washington, with all
the information required, including a copy of the
Certificate of Islamic
Divorce.
No reference is made to a divorce judgment
[26]
.

[
26
]

The Plaintiff’s expert specifies that the Imam
may request a medical certificate regarding the wife’s pregnancy and verify if
the husband fulfils his financial obligations of marriage towards her, unless
the wife consents otherwise, but has no other discretion if the husband asks
for religious divorce
[27]
.

[
27
]

Here, these conditions are met since the Plaintiff
is not pregnant, and that she has renounced spousal support and accepts the
risk of postponing the Mahr issue, subject to the Court's decision in the
divorce judgment
[28]
.

[
28
]

In the next step, the husband needs to fill out
forms available on the website of the
Interest Section of the Islamic
Republic of Iran in the Embassy of Pakistan
, located in Washington DC, USA
[29]
,
to get them to register the Islamic divorce. According to the Plaintiff’s
expert report and testimony
[30]
,
to remove existing barriers to obtaining a religious divorce, it is for the Defendant
to:

a. Mandate
the Plaintiff to act on his behalf to apply for the divorce by providing her with
a specific
Power of attorney to divorce
[31]
. The Defendant would do so via the website of the
Interest Section of the Islamic Republic of Iran
in Washington, D.C., USA;

or

b. Present himself with the
Plaintiff, when required, at an Islamic Center or before a licensed Imam who
has the knowledge of Islamic law, for the execution of the religious divorce;

and

c. Provide
all required documents and attend the virtual meeting when requested in order to
register the religious divorce with the
Interest
Section of the Islamic Republic of Iran
in
Washington;

and

d. Pay his share of the necessary costs
[approximately USD 200] for the execution and registration of the religious divorce.

[
29
]

In reply, the Defendant’s expert suggests that
the Imam cannot pronounce religious divorce before the civil divorce and would
not. Despite the distinct procedure that the Note appears to allow, she
considers that an Imam may still require the civil judgment, in accordance with
the two steps of the
Family Protection Law
in Iran. In any event, if an Imam
does not ask for a divorce judgment, she raises that the Iranian authority would
refuse to register the certificate and may annul it. Consequently, the parties
would be still deemed married in Iran.

[
30
]

Obviously, the opinion of the Defendant's expert
is based on the application of Iranian law, despite the specific procedure
permitted by the Note to section 15 of the
Family Protection Law
, and on
assumptions (including imams’ presumed discretion) which are not supported by
practical experience with this distinct procedure, otherwise known and explained
by the Plaintiff's expert, whose opinion is in line with those of the experts
retained by the Court in similar matters
[32]
.

[
31
]

Finally, it should be remembered that the
purpose of the Court’s discretionary powers is to prevent spouse’s refusal to
accept a religious divorce being used as a bargaining tool to obtain
concessions on parenting time, support or financial arrangements in the civil
divorce.
Section
21.1
of
the
Divorce Act
is a way of levelling the playing field
during the instance
[33]
.

[
32
]

As a result, the Defendant's position appears to
contradict this objective,
[34]

as explained in
Droit de la famille 231185
[35]
:

[37]    Comme on
l’a évoqué précédemment, l’une des raisons pour l’adoption de cette disposition
de la
Loi sur le divorce
, était pour empêcher
l’un des époux de se servir de son refus comme outil de marchandage pour
obtenir des concessions dans l’instance de divorce. Or, on voit mal l’utilité
d’une telle mesure si celle-ci ne pouvait être utilisée qu’une fois le divorce
civil prononcé.

[
33
]

The Defendant claims that he believed that he
was unable to obtain the religious divorce for legal and religious reasons out
of his control. But his affidavits
[36]

demonstrate that the Defendant is mostly preoccupied by the Plaintiff’s claim
of the Mahr and other accessory measures, insists on settling all issues
relating to the marriage before granting a religious divorce, afraid of loosing
all his rights and invoking financial consequences and obligations for him. Clearly,
the Defendant is using the refusal to consent to religious divorce as leverage
to extract concessions in the context of a civil divorce.

[
34
]

For these reasons, the Court concludes that the
Plaintiff’s Demand under
section 21.1
of the
Divorce Act
is well
founded, and that she is entitled to request the lifting of barriers to obtain
a religious divorce. Therefore, the Court can exercise the discretionary powers
provided for at
section 21.1 (3)
of the
Divorce Act
to dismiss the
Defendant’s proceedings
[37]
.
However, in the light of the decision of the Court of Appeal in
Droit de la
famille — 112747
[38]
,
the Court considers it appropriate to make the dismissal of the Defendant's
proceedings subject to the granting of a last delay to enable the Defendant to
remove barriers. Considering that he Plaintiff's related conclusion is too
general, making enforcement difficult, the Court makes the clarifications
deemed appropriate in the conclusions of the present judgment.

[
35
]

In the meantime, it is undeniable that the
Plaintiff has suffered damages due to the Defendant’s faulty refusal, as she
cannot travel safely and consequently, has not seen her parents and relatives for
3 years now. She lives with the stress, anxiety and fear of never returning to
her country of origin, of never seeing her ageing parents again.

[
36
]

Consequently, the sum of $5,000 is awarded to
compensate for the Plaintiff's suffering since the filing of her modified
application on October 2023, perpetuated by the Defendant's repeated refusal.

[
37
]

If the Defendant persists in refusing to provide
the Plaintiff with the documents and collaboration she needs to apply for and
obtain an Iranian divorce, further compensatory damages may be claimed. As for
punitive damages, these issues should be left to the discretion of the divorce
judge, in the light of all the evidence
[39]
.

[
38
]

Finally, the Defendant categorically denied ever
imposing a travel ban on the Plaintiff, nor having any intention to do so. His
undertakings must be retained in our conclusions.

WHEREFORE, THE
COURT:

[
39
]

GRANTS
in part the
Plaintiff’s
Demand to lift
the religious
barriers to remarry, to lift the travel ban and damages
filed on January 13, 2025;

[
40
]

DISMISSES
all the
Defendant’s demands, pleadings, defences and counter demands before the
Superior Court in the present divorce file unless, before May 7, 2025, he
provides the Plaintiff with the
Power of attorney to
divorce
and/or all required documents, appears
before a licensed Imam for the execution of the religious divorce, attends the
virtual meeting requested in order to register the religious divorce with the
Interest
Section of the Islamic Republic of Iran
in Washington and pays his share of
the necessary costs for the execution and registration of the religious divorce;

[
41
]

ORDERS
the
Defendant to pay $5 000 to the Plaintiff, with legal interest at and the
additional indemnity pursuant to the provisions of article 1619 C.C.Q. from the
service of the application;

[
42
]

REFERS
the
Plaintiff’s claim for future and punitive damages to the divorce judge;

[
43
]

TAKES ACT
that
the Defendant states that he has never imposed a travel ban on the Plaintiff
and undertakes never to do so, it being understood that in any event he
undertakes to give permission to the Iranian authority for the Plaintiff to
leave, if required, and
ORDERS
him to abide by it;

[
44
]

WITH LEGAL COSTS
.
